title: You Might Be Breaking a Rule of Communication and Don't Know It
author: Damien Gauthier
summary: Damien Gauthier, a speaking coach, borrows Paul Grice's cooperative principle from the philosophy of language and turns it into a practical test for presentations. He argues that every speaker enters an unspoken deal with an audience, who assume the speaker is trying to help them understand rather than confuse them or waste their time. The essay walks through Grice's four maxims of quantity, quality, relation, and manner, pairing each with a common failure from boardrooms, pitches, and rehearsals. Gauthier then adds Grice's notion of flouting, the deliberate breaking of a maxim that the listener is meant to notice and interpret. His conclusion is that the best speakers are not rule followers but people who know exactly which rule they are bending and why. The piece closes by converting the maxims into a four-question rehearsal checklist to run before worrying about voice or slides.
points: Under pressure, speakers instinctively add more slides, caveats, and data, but violating the maxim of quantity leaves the audience lost, and a lost audience starts doubting.
Trust is built claim by claim and can be lost in one sentence, so a single rounded or unchecked number exposed in Q&A can undo a whole presentation.
Relevance failures are often true and even interesting content delivered at the wrong moment, like a company history offered in answer to 'why should we pick you'.
Flouting a maxim on purpose, such as answering 'It was a meeting', communicates powerfully precisely because the listener notices the rule being broken.
Before rehearsing delivery, test the message with four questions on amount, evidence, relevance, and order.
quotes: When two people talk, they are making a small, unspoken agreement to cooperate: I will try to give you what you need to understand me, and you will assume I am trying to help you, not confuse you or waste your time. He called this the cooperative principle.

The instinct under pressure is almost always to add more: more slides, more caveats, more data, as if volume were proof of effort. It usually has the opposite effect. The audience does not walk away impressed. They walk away lost, and a lost audience stops listening and starts doubting.
That single moment can undo forty minutes of good work, because trust does not average out. It is built maxim by maxim, and it can be lost in one sentence.
None of it is false. None of it is even boring, necessarily. It is simply the wrong information for this exact moment, and the audience feels the drift even if they cannot name it.
A good idea presented out of sequence asks your audience to do the work of reassembling it themselves, in real time, while also trying to listen to your next point.

This is exactly why the best speakers I have coached are not the ones who follow every rule perfectly. They are the ones who know precisely which rule they are bending, why they are bending it, and when they have crossed from bending it to just breaking it.
Answer yes to all four, and you are not just informative. You are cooperative, in the exact sense Grice meant it. And cooperative is what makes a room actually want to keep listening.
